title: Learning to Choose: Finding Meaning in the Work
author: Jennifer W. Shewmaker
summary: Jennifer Shewmaker, writing from a first-year seminar context at Lipscomb University, asks why students would choose to do hard thinking themselves when AI can produce an answer in seconds. She recounts Andy Crouch's keynote at Calvin University, in which he asked whether higher education could create experiences so formative that students stop wanting 'the magic', and illustrates it with Harry digging Dobby's grave by hand in the Deathly Hallows, where the effort itself expresses love. Shewmaker realises that much AI-in-education conversation has focused on stopping students avoiding work rather than on what would make them want to stay with it. Her example is a Compass Point session in which a dean tells a personal story of strength and vocation, and students are asked to reflect on their own purpose, work that AI could tidy but cannot replace. She concludes that educators must explain why particular work is assigned and help students connect everyday learning choices to the people they hope to become. The post is aimed at higher education, but the design question applies to any classroom.
points: The AI conversation has centred on preventing avoidance; the more productive question is what makes students want to do the thinking themselves.
Effort can be an expression of value, as in Harry digging Dobby's grave without magic, so tasks need enough meaning to warrant doing them by hand.
Design shared experiences, such as a speaker's story followed by a personal reflection, where AI can polish an output but cannot supply the student's own meaning.
Explaining why a task is assigned will not persuade every student but gives them a reason to persist and a basis for deciding how to use AI.
Educators should regularly ask what work they require students to do themselves and how they help students see why it matters.
quotes: He asked us to consider, what if we could build an experience that was so formative for our students that they began to not want the magic, or the easier answer?
I realized at that moment how much of our conversations had centered on preventing students from avoiding the work. But, I had spent less time asking what would make them want to stay with it.
What moves me about this scene is the way Harry’s physical effort becomes an expression of love and gratitude for his friend.
The thing I’m mulling over right now is this: How do we create learning experiences that hold enough meaning so that our students commit to doing the work themselves?

AI might help a student organize a reflection or the story they wanted to share, but students still need to consider what their experiences mean and how another person’s story might challenge their own viewpoint.
Understanding a task’s purpose will not make everyone embrace it. But, it can give students a reason to persist and a basis for deciding how to engage in a learning activity.
We need to explain why we assign particular work and help students recognize what they are learning through it.
